session.research_context: I am a PhD student in NLP moving into HCI. My project studies how non-expert users write prompts for LLM-based tools, and I plan to run a user study.

messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: The paper introduces PromptScaffold, a prompt editor with four template slots (role, task, examples, output format) to help non-expert users write LLM prompts. In a 16-participant within-subjects lab study, prompts written with the template scored higher on an automatic task score (0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence (4.1 vs. 3.4), though they took somewhat longer (7.5 vs. 6.2 minutes).

sections.title: What the authors built
sections.text: PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots: role, task, examples and output format, each with a short hint and example. The editor assembles these into one prompt that users can preview and edit, and a side panel shows model outputs for test inputs the user provides.

sections.title: Key findings and their limits
sections.text: Mean task score was 0.74 with PromptScaffold and 0.61 with free-form prompts, with the largest gain on topic labelling. Interviews found 12 participants said the examples slot was most useful, while six said the role slot felt artificial. The authors note the template did not teach participants why each slot mattered, and several filled slots mechanically.

sections.title: Caveats before relying on the results
sections.text: The sample was small and homogeneous (16 university students, mostly from computing), the session was a single 70-minute lab session, and only three tasks and one LLM were used. Success was measured by an automatic score and self-reported confidence. The limitations paragraph also mentions a follow-up study with 412 participants that replicated the results, but no details of that study appear in the retrieved passages, so I cannot verify it.

sections.title: Possible relevance to your user study
sections.text: For a study of how non-expert users write prompts, the paper's observation that users filled slots mechanically and copied hint text suggests you may want to measure prompt content quality, not only task scores. Its use of self-reported confidence and automatic scoring could be a starting point, but you would likely need your own measures and a more diverse sample.

sources.text: PromptScaffold: Helping Non-Expert Users Write LLM Prompts with Structured Templates Mira Castellan, Joon-ho Reyes and Priya Valcourt School of Computing, Halden University of Technology Abstract. People without training in machine learning increasingly write prompts for large language model (LLM) tools, but often struggle to state the task, give examples and specify the output format. We present PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through a structured template with four slots: role, task, examples and output format. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants who completed three predefined tasks, prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher automatic task score than free-form prompts (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence. We discuss what the template helped with, where it constrained participants, and the limits of a single short lab study. 1 Introduction LLM-based tools let anyone describe a task in natural language, yet writing an effective prompt remains difficult for people without machine-learning experience.

sources.text: 2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples. Studies of prompt writing describe non-experts as relying on trial and error and on conversational phrasing. Prompt libraries and prompt-pattern catalogues offer reusable structures, but they are usually written for developers and have rarely been evaluated with non-expert users in a controlled setting. 3 The PromptScaffold Editor PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots. The role slot states who the model should act as. The task slot describes what to do, with a hint to name the input and the goal. The examples slot asks for one to three inputoutput pairs, and the output format slot asks how the answer should be structured. Each slot shows a short hint and an example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that the user can preview and edit freely before running it. A side panel shows the model's output for a small set of test inputs that the user provides. 4 Study Participants. We recruited 16 participants (9 women, 7 men, aged 19 to 27) through university mailing lists.

It did not teach participants why these parts mattered: several filled the slots mechanically. Designers of prompt tools for non-experts may therefore want to explain the purpose of each slot and let users drop slots that do not fit the task. 7 Limitations Our findings have three main limitations. First, the sample was small and homogeneous: 16 university students, most of them from computing courses, so the results may not hold for older users or for people outside a university. Second, each participant used PromptScaffold in a single 70-minute lab session; we did not study long-term or real-world use, and novelty may have raised confidence. Third, we used only three predefined classification and summarisation tasks and one LLM, and measured success only with an automatic task score and self-reported confidence. Open-ended tasks, other models and expert ratings of prompt quality may give different results. A follow-up study with 412 participants from the general public in five countries replicated these results and resolved the limitations above.

Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. Condition order was counterbalanced, and parallel task versions were used so that no participant saw the same inputs twice. All prompts were run on one LLM with fixed settings. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. After each condition, participants rated their confidence in their prompts on a 7-point scale. We also recorded the time to the final prompt and held a short interview at the end of the session. 5 Results Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1).
